rationale: B wins because it leaves fewer traps for a founder to step on. Its "Why local-currency reimbursement is the hard part of going global, not the card itself" pulls a real mechanic out of the update and then admits the proof burden, while A's "multinational-payroll problem hits mid-size companies" wanders into payroll and mid-size territory the facts never supplied. A has the sharper private-market idea, but strong proof memos do not pay for unsupported headlines.
gaps_in_A: "multinational-payroll problem hits mid-size companies" imports payroll and mid-size-company framing that are not in the update. Expense reimbursement is not payroll; do not make the reporter correct your category error.
"Ramp can't copy quickly" is a confident competitive claim without evidence. The set later asks for Ramp coverage proof, which is good, but the headline has already overpromised.

"distributed hiring made every Series B a multi-country employer" is invented trend wallpaper. The update says venture-backed startups are customers; it does not say every Series B is global or that distributed hiring caused the pain.
"employees front costs on personal cards and wait on FX-mangled reimbursements" may be true in the world, but it is not supplied here. It belongs as a customer-proof request, not as premise.
gaps_in_B: "one global spend stack" is a useful shorthand, but it extrapolates from "top enterprise customer request." It needs customer proof before it becomes the spine of the pitch.
"how incumbents (traditional card issuers) get squeezed" is too declarative. The update says Brex competes with incumbents; it does not prove pressure on them.

"the hard part of going global, not the card itself" is a strong infrastructure angle, but it still asserts a hierarchy the facts do not prove. Keep it framed as a question unless Brex can explain the mechanics.

It missed A's better financial-scrutiny lane: "A $12.3B private fintech is spending on 50-country expansion without disclosing whether it makes money." B asks the profitability question but leaves a real business/markets angle on the table.
